About: Michelson–Morley Interferometer (3D)

About This Simulation

This interactive 3D simulation reproduces the Michelson–Morley experiment (1887) as it was actually built: the optics are bolted to a massive stone slab that floats on liquid mercury in an annular cast-iron trough on a brick pier, so the whole apparatus can be rotated smoothly.

Light from the source is split by a half-silvered mirror at 45° (the beam splitter, BS). One beam passes through a compensating plate to mirror M₁; the other reflects to mirror M₂. The compensator is an identical, unsilvered copy of the splitter, so both beams traverse the same thickness of glass — without it, white-light fringes could not be seen. The returning beams recombine at BS and interfere in the telescope detector.

In the 19th century, physicists believed light traveled through a medium called the “luminiferous aether.” If so, the Earth’s motion through this aether would create a “wind” that changes the effective speed of light differently in each arm, producing a measurable fringe shift when the slab is rotated.

Aether Prediction mode shows the expected fringe shift using Galilean velocity addition — this prediction is wrong.

Actual (Relativity) mode shows the real result: no fringe shift at any angle. FitzGerald and Lorentz first explained this with an ad-hoc length contraction of the arm along the motion; Einstein’s Special Relativity (1905) explained it fundamentally — the speed of light is the same in all directions for every inertial observer.

β (v/c) is fixed at Earth’s real orbital speed (β ≈ 9.93×10⁻⁵). The effect is minuscule: with ~11 m arms the predicted round-trip difference is only a few hundred attoseconds, so the readout shows it in scientific notation / attoseconds (and it is exactly 0 in Actual mode — the null result). Guided Inquiry

1 · The interferometer

Let’s start with the apparatus itself. A single beam is split at a half-silvered mirror into two beams that travel equal lengths L down perpendicular arms, reflect off mirrors A and B, and recombine. If light were carried by a stationary ether, the Earth's orbital motion of about 30 km/s would blow that ether through the apparatus at speed v, giving β = v/c ≈ 1×10−4.

For now, the table is held at θ = 0°, with arm A lying along the wind and arm B across it.

2 · Out and back along the wind

Let’s follow one beam first. Light runs the length of arm A with the wind, reflects, and returns against it. Compared with the same round trip in still ether, how long do you think the trip takes?

3 · Across the wind

Now for the other arm. Arm B points across the wind. Compared with the same round trip in still ether — and with arm A’s trip along the wind — what do you think arm B takes?

4 · Turning the table

Here’s where the stone table comes in. It floats on mercury, so it can be turned to any angle θ. At θ = 90° arm B lies along the wind and arm A across it. What do you think the ether model predicts for A − B while θ runs from 0° to 90°?

Now turn the table yourself and follow how the A − B difference changes.

5 · What the experiment found

Now for the real thing. In 1887 Michelson and Morley turned the table through full revolutions, day and night, across the seasons. Their apparatus could resolve about one fortieth of the predicted 0.4-fringe swing. What do you think they measured?

6 · The null result

So here’s how the puzzle resolves. With c the same in every direction for every inertial observer, both arms take exactly 2L/c whatever the angle, so A − B = 0 at every θ. That’s Einstein’s second postulate, the assumption special relativity is built on.

Go ahead and turn the table through a full revolution: you’ll see the difference stays zero.

The Physics

The Michelson–Morley experiment · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim times light on a round trip down each of two perpendicular arms, first as the ether theory would have it (Aether mode), then with light at c in every direction (Actual mode). That is the Michelson–Morley experiment, a test of whether light's speed depends on how the apparatus moves.

What you'll learn

  • How an ether wind would change each arm's round-trip time.
  • Why the experiment compares two arms and turns the table.
  • How a time difference far too small to clock becomes a shift of the fringes.
  • How the outcome is read, and which assumption it puts in doubt.
The apparatus at θ = 0°: arm A along the wind, arm B across it, both of length L. Not to scale.

What's on screen

  • Light path: Source, beam splitter, mirrors M₁ (arm A) and M₂ (arm B), telescope detector. The beam takes its colour from λ.
  • Red arrows: the ether wind (Aether mode only). At θ = 0° it blows along arm A.
  • Table angle θ: the degree scale on the floor and the θ tag at the bottom left.
  • Round-trip panel (top right): each arm's round-trip time and A − B, headed by the mode.
  • Statistics (foot of the sidebar): the path change Δℓ and the fringe shift ΔN, as numbers. The sim does not draw the fringes.

Fixed: the wind speed. It is set to Earth's orbital speed, v ≈ 29.8 km/s, so β = v/c = 9.93×10⁻⁵, and it is not adjustable.

03

Out and back along the wind

The ether theory says light travels at c relative to a stationary ether. Earth moves through that ether, so the apparatus feels a wind of speed v, with β = v/c. Along arm A, light goes out with the wind at c + v and back against it at c − v.

Arm A, along the wind: the sum of the two legs.

The two legs do not cancel. The slow leg lasts longer than the fast leg saves, so the round trip is longer than the still-ether time 2L/c. For L = 11 m, 2L/c = 73.4 ns and the extra is 724 as (1 as = 10⁻¹⁸ s).

Key idea. A wind along the arm never gives back the time it takes. Against-and-with is slower than still air.
See itSwitch to Simplified view with the table at θ = 0°, so the one arm shown lies along the wind. Watch for: the "Excess over c-limit (2L/c)" row reading 724 as when L = 11 m.
04

Across the wind the arm is slowed too

Arm B lies across the wind. Aimed straight across, a beam would be swept downstream, so it must be aimed upstream. Only √(c² − v²) of its speed is left to cross the arm.

Arm B, across the wind.
Both arms at L = 11 m. The wind is drawn far larger than β = 9.93×10⁻⁵; at true size the triangle would look like a straight line.

So both arms are slowed. To leading order in β², arm B loses half of what arm A loses: 362 as against 724 as. What the experiment looks for is the difference, A − B = 362 as.

Lecture 7's aeroplane example has the same ordering: 400 km at 100 km/h takes 8 h in still air, 10 h across a 60 km/h wind and 12.5 h along it.

See itKeep Simplified view and turn the table to θ = 90°, so the arm lies across the wind. Watch for: the Excess row falling to 362 as, half of its value along the wind, when L = 11 m.
05

Turning the table swaps the arms

An arm at angle φ to the wind takes:

One arm at any angle φ to the wind. Both arms of the sim use this.

Arm A sits at θ and arm B at θ + 90°, so turning the table swaps sin² and cos² between them. To leading order, A − B ≈ (Lβ²/c) cos 2θ. For L = 11 m that is +362 as at 0°, zero at 45° and −362 as at 90°.

The table has to turn because the arms of a real apparatus are never exactly equal, and there is no "wind off" setting to compare with. Only the change under rotation can be measured, so the sim's Δℓ and ΔN are referenced to θ = 0°.

See itAuto Rotate the table from θ = 0° in Aether mode. Watch for: the A − B row falling from +362 as through about 0 near 45° to −362 as at 90° (L = 11 m).
06

Fringes turn a time difference into a shift

A difference of 362 as is 3.6×10⁻¹⁶ s, and no clock reads that. Light does: the two beams recombine, and one fringe is one wavelength of path difference. Multiplying the time difference by c gives the path difference, and dividing by λ gives fringes (t₁ and t₂ are the round trips of arms A and B).

Fringe shift from turning the table through 90°, at leading order.
L λ

These sliders move the sim too.

At L = 11 m and λ = 550 nm, c(t₁ − t₂) is +108 nm (0.2 fringe) at 0° and −108 nm at 90°. The sim reports the change from θ = 0°: Δℓ = −217 nm and ΔN = −0.394 at 90°. It never goes positive. The shift grows in proportion to L and shrinks as λ grows.

See itTurn the table to θ = 90° in Aether mode and read the fringe shift. Watch for: ΔN in Statistics reading −0.394 when L = 11 m and λ = 550 nm.
07

What 1887 found

Michelson and Morley folded their light path with mirrors to an effective arm length near 11 m and turned the apparatus through full revolutions on several days in 1887. At λ = 550 nm the ether prediction was about 0.4 fringe between 0° and 90°. They could resolve about one fortieth of that, 0.01 fringe.

Dashed: the ether prediction ΔN(θ) at L = 11 m, λ = 550 nm. The blue band is the 0.01-fringe resolution, drawn to scale.

They found no shift at any orientation, within that precision. The sim's Actual mode shows that outcome: in the apparatus's own frame light travels at c in every direction, so both arms take 2L/c at every θ.

The second postulate, in the form this experiment tests.

The result forces a choice between two things physicists believed: the principle of relativity, and Galilean velocity addition with absolute time. Relativity keeps the first and gives up the second.

See itSwitch to Actual mode and turn the table. Watch for: A − B staying at 0 s at every angle.
08

Where it matters

  • Gravitational-wave detectors. LIGO is a Michelson interferometer with 4 km arms. It reads changes in the difference of the two arm lengths, far smaller than a proton's width.
  • Tests of relativity. Modern versions use lasers in rotating optical cavities and limit any direction dependence of the speed of light to about one part in 10¹⁷.
  • Spectrometers. A Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer is a Michelson interferometer with one moving mirror. Counting fringes as the mirror moves gives the light's spectrum.
Go deeper: the rescue that hides the shift, and why relativity needs no rescue
  • FitzGerald and Lorentz proposed that the arm along the wind shortens to L√(1 − β²). Then t∥ = 2L√(1 − β²)/(c(1 − β²)) = (2L/c)/√(1 − β²), which equals t⊥ exactly, so no shift appears. It fits the result but does not explain it.
  • In relativity there is no preferred frame. In the apparatus's own frame both arms have length L and light moves at c, so both round trips are 2L/c. Frames in which the apparatus moves do show contraction, with no ether needed.
09

Summary

In one line. Compare two light round trips at right angles. If light travelled at c relative to an ether, turning the table would change the fringe count by about 0.4, and Michelson and Morley saw no such shift.

Key points

  • In an ether wind the round trips are (2L/c)/(1 − β²) along the wind and (2L/c)/√(1 − β²) across it. Both exceed 2L/c.
  • Turning the table swaps the two arms. A − B follows cos 2θ, and only that change can be measured.
  • The fringe shift between 0° and 90° is about 2Lβ²/λ: 0.394 at L = 11 m, λ = 550 nm.
  • The measured shift was far smaller than predicted, which puts Galilean velocity addition in doubt.

Common mix-ups

  • "The out-and-back legs cancel." They do not. The slow leg lasts longer than the fast leg saves.
  • "A wind across the arm does nothing." It slows arm B by half as much as arm A.
  • "They simply were not sensitive enough." They could resolve about one fortieth of the predicted 0.4 fringe.

Things to try on your own

  • In Simplified view, step the table through 0°, 45° and 90° and note the Excess row.
  • Set λ = 700 nm, then adjust L until ΔN at 90° is −0.394 again.
  • In Aether mode, find the angles where A − B is zero, then compare with Actual mode.
